corrections.caveats: The paper (ICPP '24, 'Massively Parallel Inverse Block-sorting Transforms for bzip2 Decompression on GPUs', pp. 856-865, DOI 10.1145/3673038.3673067 cited by the README) is behind blocked hosts (doi.org, dl.acm.org, researchgate and the JGU HPC group site returned EGRESS_BLOCKED; no PDF mirror in github.com/weissenberger, whose four public repos are gpuhd, multians, bzip2gpu and HIPSW4). The numbers come from a WebSearch snippet seen by the search agent only; the verifier's three queries did not reproduce it, so they are snippet-only and the tier is capped at C until someone reads the paper (likely B; fix the baseline name then). The snippet's 6.1x is for one stage (iBWT) against an unnamed multicore CPU implementation, and the 11.62 GB/s DGX H100 figure carries no baseline, so a win over bzip2, pbzip2 or lbzip2 on whole-archive decompression is not confirmed. The repo has no timing or benchmark code: src/main.cc only loads the file, calls bz2gpu::decode_stream, copies the output to the host and writes it, so the paper's throughput numbers cannot be reproduced from the repo as published; whether the GB/s figures include the host-to-device input copy, the CPU-side parser (parser::parse and build_tables run on the host with OpenMP) or the device-to-host output copy is unknown, and the README notes that uncompressed output is kept in device memory. Repo is explicitly 'auxiliary material for our publication and is not suitable for production use'. Block and stream CRC32s are never verified: a grep of all seven src files (bz2gpu.cc, decoder.cu, ibwt.cu, imtf.cu, main.cc, parser.cc, rle.cu) finds the checksum only parsed into block_checksums (parser.cc lines 220-243), matching the README TODO 'stream error detection (parsing, checksums,...)', so corrupt input is not detected. main.cc reads argv[1] and argv[2] without checking argc. Streams are limited to 2^31 - 1 uncompressed bytes (no batched execution yet). Only 2 commits (2024-07-15, 2024-07-16), no unit tests (TODO), only a 10 MB test file (test/lichess_puzzles_10M.bz2). src/rle.cu and include/thrust_custom_alloc.cuh carry modified Thrust code under Apache-2.0 with LLVM exceptions; the rest is MIT.

notes: Real peer-reviewed project (ICPP 2024) but every number is from a search snippet I could not reproduce, and the repo has no benchmark harness; kept at C with benchmark_url set to the README-cited DOI. Shortcomings to record: snippet-only numbers, unnamed CPU baseline and stage-only 6.1x, no timing code in the repo, CRC32 never checked (confirmed across all seven source files including the .cu kernels), research prototype limited to 2^31-1 bytes. Paper-access retier candidate (likely B).

tier_reason: The hat-trie README benchmark section lists tsl::array_map and std::unordered_map rows on the same harness; the benchmark code is public (gist Tessil/72e11891fc155f5b2eb53de22cbc4053: bench.cpp plus Makefile with CXXFLAGS -std=c++11 -march=native -DNDEBUG -O3 -lcityhash), compiler GCC 6.3 and CPU Intel i5-5200u are stated. Same evidence that holds the already-listed tsl::htrie_map at tier A.

corrections.caveats: The numbers are on the hat-trie README benchmark section (the array-hash README only links to the author's blog benchmark at tessil.github.io, which is egress-blocked here and was not read, and to the hat-trie page). Benchmark dates from 2017: GCC 6.3, a dual-core ultrabook CPU (i5-5200u, 8 GB), and the comparison set is std::unordered_map, tsl::hopscotch_map, google::dense_hash_map, spp::sparse_hash_map and the tries; absl::flat_hash_map and tsl::robin_map are not in the table, so the listed absl and robin baselines are not covered. Baseline stdlib is libstdc++ by inference (GCC on Debian Stretch), not stated outright. std::unordered_map is keyed on std::string (32 bytes minimum per key), which handicaps it on memory by design, and its insert wrapper in the gist (map.insert({str, value})) builds a std::pair<const std::string, int> temporary and then copies the const key into the node, so each baseline insert copies the key twice (small bias against the baseline; the same flaw is recorded for tsl::htrie_map). Insert is not faster without reserve (603.94 vs 590.88 ns/key on Wikipedia, 545.82 vs 554.02 on Askitis), and lookups are slower than tsl::hopscotch_map (138.24 vs 119.49 ns/key on Wikipedia) and about equal on Askitis, where google::dense_hash_map reads slightly faster (43.62, or 43.09 with reserve, vs 46.41). The Askitis read set (skew1_1) repeats keys heavily (177,999,203 lookups over short keys averaging 5.06 bytes), which favours cache-resident structures. The README says best of 20 runs, but the gist's Makefile builds one binary per structure and bench.cpp times a single pass with std::chrono::high_resolution_clock, so the 20-run driver is not public. Memory is read from /proc/self/statm (resident pages), and peak memory with array_map without reserve (823.54 MiB) is well above final memory (678.73 MiB) because rehash must copy strings (the README notes rehash is slow and needs spare memory). Lookups only test presence (nb_found counter), the value is not read. Flags were read through WebFetch summaries of the gist page, not a raw download (gist.githubusercontent.com is blocked).

notes: All eight claimed figures match the hat-trie README rows exactly (Wikipedia shuffled and Askitis tables); metadata confirmed (MIT, 187 stars, last commit 2025-11-02, active). Not a duplicate: tsl::htrie_map (wave 9 verified, tier A) vendors array-hash under include/tsl/array-hash, but array_map is a separate standalone hash map with its own repo. Shortcomings to record: insert without reserve not faster, slower reads than tsl::hopscotch_map and dense_hash_map, 2017 hardware and no modern baselines (absl, robin_map), README's best-of-20 not in the public harness, baseline insert copies the key twice.
